transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-17 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Rao (Horizon), Ben Alvarez (Horizon), Sofia Marin (Horizon)

Auto Summary: Quick hosted API live test showing streaming partial responses, param tuning, retry strategy, and console pointers. Security questions re: SOC2/SAML/KMS. Agreed POC and next steps.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood inference team, and Liam is our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Priya: Good, thanks. Quick note — we're timeboxed to ~45 minutes, but we'll be flexible. I'm Priya, lead of data at Horizon.
[00:20] Ben: Ben, platform. We're mostly focused on API behavior and how it fits into our event pipeline.
[00:26] Sofia: Sofia, product. I'll be taking notes on UX and latency.
[00:30] Liam (Redwood SE): Great. Today we'll do a hands-on with the hosted gen endpoint — streaming, key generation params, and a bit on retries and backoff. We'll also show the Console Optimize suggestions where it makes sense.
[00:45] Maya: We'll link the deck and the bench script in the follow-up. If you want, Liam can start the live demo where we fire a few prompts and show streams and how partial chunks look.
[00:54] Priya: Yes please, especially interested in prefix caching and whether repeated patient-note prompts will be cheaper.
[01:05] Liam: Cool. I'm in the Console, selecting model "redwood-llama-2-13b-opt" — note this is for demo, actual POC we'll pick the variant you prefer. I'm going to open the sandbox curl client and run a chat generate with streaming=true.
[01:22] Liam: (typing) Sending prompt now — you'll see partial tokens come in: first chunk ... and second chunk ... that's the server streaming chunked responses. On our side we provide an SSE/HTTP2 chunked stream and SDK streaming helpers for Node/Python.
[01:38] Ben: Quick question — what happens if a stream drops mid-response? Do you retry idempotently?
[01:45] Liam: Good question. For non-idempotent generation we recommend clients implement a token-wise reconciliation strategy; Redwood also supports automatic resume if the session id and KV cache are available. For hosted we keep ephemeral KV cache per request; if you need durable KV reuse across calls you can enable prefix caching which Redwood handles by keying on prompt hash.
[02:05] Priya: Is that prefix caching encrypted? We have PHI so encryption at rest is a must.
[02:10] Maya: Yes — data at rest is encrypted using customer-managed KMS in our Dedicated/Private options; for hosted we use HSM-backed KMS and can provide a key-wrapping profile in the security pack. We'll attach the KMS note in the doc.
[02:28] Sofia: And SSO? We use Okta and need SAML SSO for console access.
[02:33] Maya: SAML/SSO is supported for Console; we'll send the SAML config guide. Also, SOC 2 type II report is available — we'll share that.
[02:44] Liam: Back to streaming — here's a second example with partial safety filters applied. Notice the stream includes meta events for content policy flags, so you can react mid-stream.
[03:06] Ben: About params — can you show temperature and top_p effects quickly?
[03:10] Liam: Sure. Running same prompt with temperature 0.0, 0.7, 1.2. Temp 0 gives deterministic replies; 0.7 adds variance; 1.2 more creative but higher risk. For many clinical summarization tasks we'd recommend temperature 0-0.2 plus constrained top_p. Also watch max_tokens — we cap at 2048 by default for this model, but config is per model variant.
[03:42] Priya: We do long templates with patient history — will the token limit impact us?
[03:46] Liam: If your prompts are prefix-heavy, enable prefix/KV cache and use the long-context variant. The console Optimize tab will recommend quantization or long-context models depending on your average seq length.
[03:58] Maya: Also worth mentioning batching — if you have bursts of short requests we can batch with low latency impact. For throughput-sensitive pipelines, Dedicated capacity gives fixed throughput SLAs.
[04:15] Ben: Cost — how does batching and quantization affect price per token?
[04:21] Liam: Batching reduces per-token GPU overhead, so cost per token drops; quantization trades off slight quality for lower memory footprint and often lower cost. Optimize will give an estimate based on your sample prompts. We'll run a cost simulation for your sample prompts in the POC.
[04:42] Sofia: Can you demo retries now? We sometimes see transient 503s from upstream services.
[04:49] Liam: Yes. I'll simulate a transient failure by forcing a stream disconnect on our side so you can see both server and client behaviors. (simulating) You should see a retry with exponential backoff — first retry at ~200ms, then 600ms, then 1800ms, and we failover to a fallback model variant if retries exhaust.
[05:18] Ben: Do retries re-run generations (non-idempotent) or resume?
[05:22] Liam: If the client includes the conversation history and the request id, the server can resume using the cached KV state; otherwise retries may produce a new generation. We recommend client-side idempotency keys for critical workflows.
[05:35] Priya: How do you handle token accounting on retries for billing?
[05:39] Maya: We bill on tokens that were actually accepted by the server for a successful call. Partial tokens streamed and then aborted are generally not billed, but we'll include the exact billing semantics in the security/ops doc.
[05:52] Ben: Any rate limit guidance? We expect spikes after nightly batch jobs.
[05:56] Liam: Rate limits configurable per org; for spikes you can enable burst capacity or Dedicated pools. We can set per-route quotas and token-based throttles.
[06:08] Sofia: Show the Console's Optimize recommendations?
[06:11] Liam: Sure. Navigating to Console -> Optimize. Here we have suggested quantization levels, recommended model family per workload, and a simulated cost vs latency graph based on sample prompts. For your clinical summaries with long prefixes the suggestion is: use long-context variant + enable prefix cache + set temperature 0.1.
[06:35] Priya: That graph's useful. Can you export the bench results?
[06:39] Liam: Yes, we export CSV with per-token latencies and per-request breakdown. I'll attach it to the follow-up.
[06:46] Ben: For compliance we need audit logs of token usage and user-level access.
[06:50] Maya: Audit logs and token-level usage traces are part of our Enterprise package; we capture request metadata, route, model version and user id. We'll include sample audit log entries in the security pack.
[07:03] Priya: On latency numbers — what SLOs are realistic for 1–2k token responses?
[07:08] Liam: On Dedicated you can get tail latencies sub-500ms for small responses; for 1–2k tokens typical server-side generation time depends on sequence length and model size — expect several seconds. We recommend streaming to improve perceived latency. Also we'll tune kernels and batching to reduce p95.
[07:30] Sofia: Does Redwood offer function-calling or structured output to help parse clinical fields?
[07:34] Liam: Yes, our chat gen supports structured outputs and function/tool calling primitives so you can constrain responses and extract JSON schema. We'll demo in the POC if you want strict field extraction.
[07:48] Ben: Any limits on concurrent streams per org?
[07:51] Maya: Default is conservative for hosted; for production you'll want to either move to a Dedicated capacity or request increased limits via support.
[07:58] Priya: We have data residency needs in EU for some clients — can you pin models to EU region?
[08:03] Maya: Hosted supports region pinning for enterprise customers; Private and Dedicated give full region control. We'll note that in the security doc.
[08:14] Liam: Switching back to failure modes — here's a sequence where the model throws a safety flag; the stream includes a policy event, client can either redact or stop. You can configure auto-block or manual review.
[08:33] Priya: That's helpful, our escalation needs manual review.
[08:36] Liam: We'll flag that in the POC config.
[08:39] Sofia: Any gotchas we should know integrating with our event-driven infra?
[08:43] Ben: We use Kafka and serverless consumers. Need idempotency and replay protection.
[08:47] Liam: For event-driven patterns, use idempotency keys and store request metadata; we can also add a tokenization step in your pipeline to estimate token usage prior to hitting Redwood to avoid surprises.
[08:59] Priya: Can we instrument devs with a lightweight SDK?
[09:02] Maya: Yes, we have Node/Python/Java SDKs with streaming helpers; Liam will share sample code.
[09:10] (brief crosstalk / typing)
[09:25] Liam: I'm going to run one more demo: long prefix + streaming + deliberate disconnect to show resume. (typing) You should see partial summary, then a reconnect and resumed tokens.
[09:45] Ben: I see it — nice. The resume behavior is clear.
[09:48] Priya: Any examples of tenant isolation with multi-tenant Hosted?
[09:52] Maya: Hosted gives logical separation and encryption in transit; for stronger isolation we recommend Dedicated. If you have strict PCI/PHI isolation, Private or Dedicated with customer-managed keys is the path.
[10:05] Sofia: Let's talk timeline — if we want a POC next week, what's needed from our side?
[10:09] Maya: Sample prompt sets (3), expected qps, target latency SLOs, and any compliance docs. We'll provision a sandbox org and grant Ben + Priya access.
[10:18] Priya: We'll collect the prompts and send by Wednesday.
[10:22] Ben: Also want the bench script so we can reproduce locally.
[10:25] Liam: I'll upload the bench script and a README with run commands.
[10:29] Maya: Ok let's recap and do a short wrap.
[10:32] Maya: Recap — we showed streaming, params tuning, retries and resume semantics, console Optimize flow, and discussed security/compliance. Agreed POC with deliverables: prompts, bench script, SOC2 docs.
[10:45] Priya: Sounds good. One last question: pricing model for trial usage?
[10:49] Maya: We'll provide a trial credit allocation and estimated cost from Optimize; longer term it's per-token plus reserved capacity options for Dedicated. I'll include an estimate for your sample workload.
[10:59] (end — quick goodbyes)
[11:02] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and links.
[11:05] Priya: Thanks, bye.
notes: Shared artifacts: demo bench script (link), SOC2 brief (link), Console optimize export (link)
